topics.title: 5.1 Floating-Point Concepts
topics.summary: The sign distinguishes positive and negative values. In common IEEE 754 binary formats, it is stored separately from exponent and fraction fields. Unlike two’s-complement integers, changing only the floating-point sign bit changes the sign of an ordinary finite value without changing its magnitude. The format also contains positive and negative zero. They compare equal in ordinary numerical comparison, but operations such as reciprocal can distinguish them under IEEE arithmetic. A diagnostic that prints only 0 can therefore hide a representational distinction relevant to numerical algorithms or branch-cut conventions. The exponent determines the power-of-two scale. Normal binary floating-point values have the form (-1)^s * (1.f) * 2^e . The stored exponent is biased so the field can represent both negative and positive exponents without a separate exponent sign bit. For binary32, the exponent field has eight bits and the normal-value bias is 127. A stored exponent of 130 therefore corresponds to an exponent of 3. Some exponent field values are reserved for zero, subnormal values, infinity, and NaN, so not every field pattern describes an ordinary normalized scale. The significand carries the significant digits. For a normalized binary value, the leading digit is always one, so common IEEE binary formats omit that leading one from storage. Binary32 stores 23 fraction bits but has 24 bits of normal-value precision. Binary64 stores 52 fraction bits and has 53 bits of normal-value precision. Precision is the number of significant bits, not the number of fixed decimal places. A value near one and a value near one billion do not have the same absolute spacing between representable neighbors. Numerical error requirements should therefore distinguish absolute error from relative error. [ R9 ]

topics.title: 5.2 IEEE 754
topics.summary: For binary32 with exponent field E from 1 through 254 and fraction field F , the represented value is (-1)^s * (1 + F/2^23) * 2^(E-127) . Read this as a signed significand multiplied by a power-of-two scale. Normalization gives a unique leading-one form for ordinary nonzero values. For example, binary 1101.01 becomes 1.10101 * 2^3 . The shift changes the exponent while preserving the value. Format calculations should identify the stored exponent and the mathematical exponent separately to avoid off-by-bias errors. The term subnormal is preferred for values historically called denormalized. When the exponent field is zero and the fraction is nonzero, binary32 uses (-1)^s * (F/2^23) * 2^-126 . There is no implicit leading one. This extends representable values gradually toward zero below the smallest normal magnitude. Subnormals provide gradual underflow but have fewer significant bits relative to their magnitude. Some execution modes flush tiny values to zero for particular operations. Such modes alter numerical behavior and must be treated as explicit configuration, not assumed equivalent to default IEEE-style arithmetic. An all-zero exponent field and zero fraction represent zero, with the sign field distinguishing positive and negative zero. Both compare equal, so a hash or serialization design that uses raw bits must decide whether these representations should remain distinct or be normalized. An exact zero result and a tiny result rounded to zero are not the same computational event. The latter can indicate lost information. Numerical diagnostics may need to examine exception flags or compare against a higher-precision reference rather than looking only at the final printed value. An all-one exponent field with a zero fraction represents infinity. Positive and negative infinity can arise from operations such as an overflowing finite result or division of a nonzero finite value by zero under the relevant floating-point environment. Infinity is not the largest finite number. It participates in comparison and arithmetic as a special value. An application that requires finite measurements should validate with a finite-value predicate rather than testing only that the input lies below one chosen threshold. Infinity can otherwise propagate through an algorithm and obscure the original failure. An all-one exponent field with a nonzero fraction represents a NaN, or “not a number.” NaNs represent invalid or unrepresentable numerical results such as certain indeterminate operations. In ordinary comparisons, a NaN is unequal even to itself, and ordered comparisons with it are false. Use a designated NaN predicate rather than equality to detect NaNs. Algorithms based on total ordering, minimum selection, or sorting need an explicit policy for them. A comparison function that violates the ordering requirements of a container or sorting algorithm can fail in ways unrelated to the original arithmetic.

topics.title: Worked example — Encoding 13.25 as binary32
topics.summary: Start with the decimal value 13.25. The integer part 13 is binary 1101 ; the fraction 0.25 is 0.01 , so the complete binary value is 1101.01 . Normalize it to 1.10101 * 2^3 . The sign is zero. The stored exponent is 3 + 127 = 130 , or binary 10000010 . The stored fraction is 10101 followed by zeros to fill 23 positions. Its numeric field is 0x540000 . Combining sign, exponent, and fraction gives the 32-bit pattern 0x41540000 . This value is exactly representable because its binary expansion terminates within the available precision. Companion listing: ch05/float_bits.c The reference platform prints 0x41540000 . The numeric interpretation of a copied representation also assumes the reference platform’s compatible integer and float byte ordering; the format checks alone do not prove every representation detail on every machine. The example inspects a platform representation rather than defining a portable wire encoding. For a second trace, add 1 to binary32 16,777,216. The exact result lies halfway between 16,777,216 and 16,777,218. Under round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, it rounds to 16,777,216. The addition occurred, but the format could not retain that unit difference. This is precision loss, not integer-style wraparound.

SLIDE 10: Worked example — Encoding 13.25 as binary32
